newsitem.title: USA: INSIGHT - Wall St navigates more perilous times.
newsitem.headline: INSIGHT - Wall St navigates more perilous times.

text.p: The Dow's dizzying record climb has crushed short sellers and sent others scurrying to the safety of blue chips, as the bull market enters a more perilous time.

Fundamentals have been shunted aside as the market moves forward on powerful momentum. While the timing of "the Big One," a crumble of the magnitude of 1,000 points, cannot be pinpointed, the periscopes have gone up for signs of deterioration. Players have also grown more sensitive to the Wall Street rumor mill, which has shifted into overdrive.

"It's a dangerous time in the market. Not for those who are long-term investors, since whatever happens (such as a stiff correction), the market will go higher over time. But it's dangerous for the ones that are in with money that belongs elsewhere and those who are short. The shorts have got to be dying," said Ehrenkrantz King Nussbaum's William LeFevre.

The Dow on Wednesday scored its 10th record closing high for the month, as it has climbed over 400 points in the past 2-1/2 weeks to about 6422 Thursday afternoon. Stocks have been aided by euphoria over a still politically divided government, evidence of a slowing economy and lower interest rates.

But the near-panic buying in some blue chips has raised some eyebrows. "We went from 130 to 159 in IBM. It's a case where this thing is going on momentum and not fundamentals," said LeFevre, a senior market analyst.

Analysts said fund managers have driven up blue chips like Intel Corp and Microsoft Corp in a bid to put money to work quickly in "safe," very liquid names in case cash needs to be raised quickly. "Who would fault a manager for buying these shares?" asked Ralph Bloch of Raymond James.
Ken Ducey, head of trading at BT Brokerage, said, "A lot of people are day-trading and that adds fuel to the fire."

"When you see GM (General Motors Corp) or Caterpillar (Inc) rising a couple of points... these are big, heavy industrials that rarely see that type of action. So people are buying, not selling. The market has eaten through supply and people are holding on to what they want," Ducey added. But he does not see "the Big One" anytime soon. "Most people think momentum is too strong, don't fight the tape. The Big One would be a 1,000 point correction and it doesn't look like it will happen again soon. People will be adjusting portfolios for the year-end."
But Bloch pointed to signs that players should look for.

"We're in a straight-up acceleration phase. In this two things happen. One is it provides the best profits in the shortest periods of time. Part of the phase is short-covering. The other part of the acceleration phase is without even a modest break, it will also yield to an upside exhaustion."

"A classic key reversal day is when the market makes a new high on huge volume and then is smacked lower at the end of the day. We could have a downside gap the next day," said Bloch, chief technical analyst at Raymond James.
Veteran analysts also scoffed at notions that "this time, it's different" due to the baby boomers' mutual fund flood.
"I've heard 'This time, it's different' in the 60s, 70s and 80s. You can depart from the fundamentals some of the time but sooner or later they catch up with you," LeFevre said.
"This time the overriding force might be mutual fund flows. But then something happens, it slows or starts flowing out (of stocks) and eventually fundamentals count," he said.
LeFevre said the Dow was now trading at 20.1 times trailing earnings, compared with 19.7 before the October 1987 crash. "It's certainly richly valued and may be overvalued."
He also saw "dangerous" times for some investors since the "rumor mill has gone into overdrive."

Recent false rumors pressuring individual stocks or the overall market include talk that Goldman Sachs' Abby Joseph Cohen made negative comments on stocks, that Goldman was downgrading Intel and that SoundView was cutting IBM.
"People out there are trying to talk this market down; whether they're short or whatever reason this rise has gotten extremely painful for them," LeFevre said.

He thinks the market "is at least entitled to a rest." While the analyst did not see a nosebleed selloff in the absence of "a big event," he ended the conversation saying, "I really think we're near something. I have that feeling."
-- Wall Street desk 212 859 1721
